name: Closed-source terminals
summary: The terminal that ships with macOS, and commercial terminals and SSH clients. Nothing is wrong with using them, and there is next to no lock-in: a terminal holds settings, not data. This entry is for people who want an open-source one anyway, or who are leaving an SSH client that keeps their host list in its own cloud.

factors: Saved profiles, colours and key bindings
Synced SSH host lists in commercial clients

export.summary: A terminal holds almost no data. Your shell configuration, history and SSH keys live in your home directory and work everywhere.

methods.name: Nothing to export
methods.detail: Shell configuration (.zshrc, .bashrc), history and the ~/.ssh directory are independent of the terminal application.

methods.name: SSH host lists
methods.detail: Commercial SSH clients can usually export their saved hosts. Turn them into entries in ~/.ssh/config, which every terminal understands.

caveats: Colour schemes need choosing again; most popular themes exist for all three alternatives

paths.verdict: The easiest switch on macOS and Linux: it looks and behaves like a native app and needs no setup.

import.summary: Install it and open it. Pick a theme and font in the config file if the defaults do not suit you.

transfers: Your shell, its configuration and history
lost: Synced host lists and credential vaults from commercial SSH clients
Windows support, if you also work there

paths.verdict: For people who work across Windows, macOS and Linux, or want to replace tmux as well.

import.summary: Install it and write a short Lua configuration file for your font, colours and key bindings. SSH hosts from ~/.ssh/config appear automatically.

transfers: Your shell, its configuration and history
SSH keys and ~/.ssh/config, used for built-in remote sessions
One configuration file shared across operating systems
lost: Synced host lists and credential vaults from commercial SSH clients

paths.verdict: For minimalists who already use tmux or a tiling window manager.

import.summary: Install it and add a small TOML file for your font and colours. If you relied on tabs or splits, set up tmux or Zellij alongside.

transfers: Your shell, its configuration and history
lost: Tabs and splits, unless you add a multiplexer
Synced host lists and credential vaults from commercial SSH clients

paths.verdict: For people who want tabs, splits, inline images and scripting built into the terminal itself, on macOS or Linux.

import.summary: Install it and set your font and colours in kitty.conf; it reloads on save and has built-in theme and font pickers. On servers that do not know its terminal type, connect with 'kitten ssh'.

transfers: Your shell, its configuration and history
Tabs, splits and window layouts, without tmux
lost: Synced host lists and credential vaults from commercial SSH clients
Windows support, if you also work there
